events.text:
No evidence found in Britannica.

The Britannica corpus (1771–1797 scans) contains no entry on the planet Neptune. I searched the Britannica side twice:

- Query "Neptune" → zero results (`low_confidence: true`, nothing found).
- Query "Neptune planet" → only a false match: [B:1250:1], headword COINAGE, whose passage mentions a "planet" only as OCR garble ("planehet") in a passage about coin dies.

This is consistent with history: Neptune was not discovered until 1846, after this edition (1st–3rd Britannica, 1771–1797).

For context only, Wikipedia's Neptune article [W:19003265:1353797681] states Neptune is "the eighth and farthest known planet orbiting the Sun... 17 times the mass of Earth... not visible to the unaided eye and... the only planet in the Solar System that was not initially observed by direct empirical observation," with its position mathematically predicted by John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier before telescopic observation. That is Wikipedia evidence, not Britannica — I have no Britannica text to compare it against.

No evidence found in Britannica.

The Britannica corpus (1771–1797 scans) contains no entry on the planet Neptune. I searched the Britannica side twice:

- Query "Neptune" → zero results (`low_confidence: true`, nothing found).
- Query "Neptune planet" → only a false match: [B:1250:1], headword COINAGE, whose passage mentions a "planet" only as OCR garble ("planehet") in a passage about coin dies.

This is consistent with history: Neptune was not discovered until 1846, after this edition (1st–3rd Britannica, 1771–1797).

For context only, Wikipedia's Neptune article [W:19003265:1353797681] states Neptune is "the eighth and farthest known planet orbiting the Sun... 17 times the mass of Earth... not visible to the unaided eye and... the only planet in the Solar System that was not initially observed by direct empirical observation," with its position mathematically predicted by John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier before telescopic observation. That is Wikipedia evidence, not Britannica — I have no Britannica text to compare it against.
